{
  "file_path": "/Users/sumeet/matrix/web/akhar/components/lessons/GlossaryLessonView.tsx",
  "content": "// Glossary — every word from the curriculum in one alphabetical list.\n// Built dynamically from CURRICULUM so it stays in sync.\nimport {\n  CURRICULUM,\n  type LetterLesson,\n  type NuktaGroupLesson,\n  type MatraLesson,\n  type MuktaLesson,\n  type ConceptLesson,\n  type ExampleWord,\n} from \"@/data/curriculum\";\nimport LetterAudio from \"@/components/LetterAudio\";\n\ninterface Entry extends ExampleWord {\n  from: string;  // which lesson contributed it\n}\n\nfunction collectWords(): Entry[] {\n  const out: Entry[] = [];\n  const seen = new Set<string>();\n  function push(w: ExampleWord, from: string) {\n    if (seen.has(w.pa)) return;\n    seen.add(w.pa);\n    out.push({ ...w, from });\n  }\n  for (const l of CURRICULUM) {\n    if (l.kind === \"letter\") {\n      const ll = l as LetterLesson;\n      for (const ex of ll.examples) push(ex, `${ll.char} (${ll.name_iso})`);\n    } else if (l.kind === \"nukta-group\") {\n      const ng = l as NuktaGroupLesson;\n      for (const n of ng.letters)\n        for (const ex of n.examples) push(ex, `${n.char} (${n.name_iso})`);\n    } else if (l.kind === \"matra\") {\n      const ml = l as MatraLesson;\n      for (const ex of ml.examples) push(ex, `${ml.matra} (${ml.name_iso})`);\n    } else if (l.kind === \"mukta\") {\n      const mu = l as MuktaLesson;\n      for (const ex of mu.examples) push(ex, \"Mukta\");\n    } else if (l.kind === \"concept\") {\n      const cl = l as ConceptLesson;\n      for (const ex of cl.examples) push(ex, `${cl.symbol} (${cl.name_iso})`);\n    }\n  }\n  // Sort alphabetically by Gurmukhi codepoints — gives a stable, intuitive order\n  out.sort((a, b) => a.pa.localeCompare(b.pa));\n  return out;\n}\n\nexport default function GlossaryLessonView() {\n  const entries = collectWords();\n  return (\n    <article>\n      <header className=\"text-center\">\n        <h1 className=\"text-3xl font-semibold text-zinc-900 dark:text-zinc-50\">\n          Glossary\n        </h1>\n        <p className=\"mx-auto mt-3 max-w-md text-sm text-zinc-500\">\n          Every word taught in the curriculum, in Gurmukhi alphabetical\n          order. {entries.length} entries. Tap any word to hear it.\n        </p>\n      </header>\n\n      <section className=\"mt-10\">\n        <ul className=\"divide-y divide-zinc-200 dark:divide-zinc-800\">\n          {entries.map((e) => (\n            <li\n              key={e.pa}\n              className=\"flex items-center gap-3 py-2\"\n            >\n              {e.emoji && (\n                <span className=\"w-6 text-center text-lg\" aria-hidden>\n                  {e.emoji}\n                </span>\n              )}\n              <span className=\"w-32 shrink-0 font-serif text-lg text-zinc-900 dark:text-zinc-50\">\n                {e.pa}\n              </span>\n              <span className=\"w-24 shrink-0 font-mono text-xs text-zinc-500\">\n                {e.iso}\n              </span>\n              <span className=\"flex-1 text-sm text-zinc-700 dark:text-zinc-300\">\n                {e.en}\n              </span>\n              <span className=\"hidden shrink-0 font-mono text-xs text-zinc-400 sm:inline\">\n                {e.from}\n              </span>\n              <LetterAudio text={e.pa} label=\"\" />\n            </li>\n          ))}\n        </ul>\n      </section>\n    </article>\n  );\n}\n"
}

# AQA GCSE Panjabi 8683 Assessment Papers

## Paper 1: Listening
- **Skill tested:** "Understanding and responding to different types of spoken language"
- **Duration:** 35 minutes (Foundation), 45 minutes (Higher)
- **Marks:** 40 (Foundation), 50 (Higher)
- **GCSE weighting:** 25%
- **Format:** Written exam with 5-minute reading time before stimulus plays
- **Tiers:** Foundation and Higher (different content)
- **Question structure:** Section A (English questions, answered in English/non-verbally); Section B (Panjabi questions, answered in Panjabi/non-verbally)

## Paper 2: Speaking
- **Skill tested:** "Communicating and interacting effectively in speech for a variety of purposes"
- **Duration:** 7–9 minutes (Foundation) + prep time; 10–12 minutes (Higher) + prep time
- **Marks:** 60 (both tiers)
- **GCSE weighting:** 25%
- **Format:** Non-exam assessment
- **Components:** Role-play (15 marks, 2 min both tiers); Photo card (15 marks, 2 min Foundation/3 min Higher); General conversation (30 marks, 3–5 min Foundation/5–7 min Higher)

## Paper 3: Reading
- **Skill tested:** "Understanding and responding to different types of written language"
- **Duration:** 45 minutes (Foundation), 1 hour (Higher)
- **Marks:** 60 (both tiers)
- **GCSE weighting:** 25%
- **Format:** Written exam
- **Question structure:** Section A (English questions); Section B (Panjabi questions); Section C (translation from Panjabi to English: minimum 35 words Foundation/50 words Higher)

## Paper 4: Writing
- **Skill tested:** "Communicating effectively in writing for a variety of purposes"
- **Duration:** 1 hour (Foundation), 1 hour 15 minutes (Higher)
- **Marks:** 50 (Foundation), 60 (Higher)
- **GCSE weighting:** 25%
- **Format:** Written exam
- **Foundation questions:** Message (8 marks); Short passage (~40 words, 16 marks); Translation (35+ words, 10 marks); Structured task (~90 words, 16 marks)
- **Higher questions:** Structured task (~90 words, 16 marks); Open-ended task (~150 words, 32 marks); Translation (50+ words, 12 marks)

# AQA GCSE Panjabi 8683 - Complete Grammar Requirements

## Foundation Tier

**Nouns**
- Single and plural forms
- Direct and oblique case forms

**Gender**
- Gender distinctions in noun forms

**Adjectives**
- "Black" (inflecting) and "red" (invariable) types
- Attributive and predicative usage
- Demonstrative: ਇਹ (proximal), ਉਹ (distal)
- Indefinite: ਕੋਈ
- Possessive adjectives and ਆਪਣਾ
- Interrogative: ਕਿਹੜਾ, ਕਿ ਸਦਾ

**Adverbs**
- Interrogative: ਕਿੱਥੇ, ਕਿਵੇਂ, ਕਿਉਂ
- Time and place adverbs
- Relative/correlative pairs (receptive only)
- Common adverbial phrases
- Particles: ਹੀ, ਵੀ, ਤਾਂ (receptive)

**Verbs - Personal Forms**
- Subjunctive: ਜਾਵਾਂ, ਕਰਾਂ
- Ordinary imperative: ਜਾਹ, ਕਰ
- Polite imperative: ਜਾਈਂ, ਕਰੀਂ (receptive)

**Verbs - Adjectival Forms**
- Imperfect participle: ਜਾਂਦਾ, ਕਰਦਾ
- Perfect participle: ਗਿਆ, ਕੀਤਾ
- Potential participal: ਜਾਣਾ, ਕਰਨਾ

**Verbs - Mixed Forms**
- Subjective + ਗਾ (future): ਜਾਵਾਂਗਾ, ਕਰਾਂਗਾ

**Verbs - Nominal Forms**
- Gerund: ਜਾਣਾ
- Conjunctive participle: stem + ਕੇ (ਜਾ ਕੇ)
- Adjectival verb forms as adjectives (receptive)

**Tense Forms**
- ਹੈ, ਸੀ conjugations

**Auxiliary Verbs**
- ਦੇ, ਲੈ, ਸਕਦੇ, ਚੁੱਕ, ਹੋ, ਰਹਿ

**Causatives**
- ਕਰਨਾ → ਕਰਾਉਣਾ → ਕਰਵਾਉਣਾ

**Imperfect Forms**
- stem + ਈ: ਕਰੀਦਾ, ਜਾਈਦਾ, ਨੱਠੀਦਾ (receptive)

**Serial Verb Constructions**
- Simple forms: ਜਾਂਦਾ ਸੀ, ਜਾ ਰਿਹਾ ਸੀ, ਜਾ ਰਿਹਾ ਹੋਵੇਗਾ

**Passive Structures**
- Perfect participle + ਜਾ: ਕੀਤਾ ਜਾਣਾ, ਪੜ੍ਹਿਆ ਜਾਂਦਾ, ਰੱਖਿਆ ਜਾਵੇਗਾ
- Verb agreement with subject, object, or no agreement

**Postpositions**
- Simple: ਤੋਂ, ਨੂੰ, ਦਾ
- Place-based: ਉੱਤੇ, ਹੇਠਾਂ, ਸਾਹਮਣੇ
- Compound: ਦੇ ਹੇਠਾਂ, ਦੇ ਸਾਹਮਣੇ
- Emphatic compound: ਦੇ ਉੱਤੇ
- ਵਾਲਾ case forms and uses

**Conjunctions**
- Coordinating: ਅਤੇ, ਪਰ
- Subordinating: ਕਿਉਂਕਿ, ਜਦ, ਜਦੋਂ

**Numbers and Quantity**
- Cardinal and ordinal numbers
- Dates and time expressions
- Fractional numbers (receptive): ਡੇਢ, ਢਾਈ, ਸਵਾ, ਪੌਣੇ, ਸਾਢੇ

---

## Higher Tier (Additional Requirements)

**Particles**
- ਤਾਂ (now active, not receptive)

**Verbs - Additional Forms**
- Adjectival verbs as adjectives: ਵਗਦਾ ਪਾਣੀ, ਟੁੱਟਿਆ ਗਲਾਸ
- Polite imperative (active): ਜਾਈਂ, ਕਰੀਂ
- Potential participle conveying imperative meaning
- Imperfect stem + ਈ (active): ਕਰੀਦਾ, ਜਾਈਦਾ, ਨੱਠੀਦਾ
- Durative/iterative with ਈ: ਕਰੀ ਜਾਓ, ਪੜ੍ਹੀ ਗਿਆ

**Auxiliary Verbs - Higher Tier**
- ਆ, ਜਾ, ਰੱਖ, ਛੱਡ

**Complex Conditional Forms**
- Imperfect participle for counterfactual: "ਜੇ ਤੂੰ ਮਿਹਨਤ ਕਰਦਾ, ਤਾਂ ਪਾਸ ਹੋ ਜਾਂਦਾ"

**Serial Verb Constructions - Extended**
- Complex forms (receptive): ਜਾ ਰਿਹਾ ਹੋਵੇਗਾ, ਬਣਦਾ ਜਾ ਰਿਹਾ ਸੀ, ਲਿਖਿਆ ਪਿਆ ਸੀ, ਬਣਾਏ ਜਾਂਦੇ ਰਹੇ ਹਨ

**Passive Structures - Extended**
- Perfect participle + ਹੋ (receptive): ਕੀਤਾ ਹੋਇਆ, ਧੋਤਾ ਹੋਇਆ, ਰੱਖਿਆ ਹੋਇਆ

**Quasi-Verb Forms**
- Receptive knowledge: ਬੈਠੇ-ਬਿਠਾਏ, ਚਲਦਿਆਂ-ਕਰਦਿਆਂ, ਕਰਦਿਆਂ ਹੋਇਆਂ

**Complex Sentences**
- Advanced subordination with relative pronouns and subordinators exemplified by constructions like complex temporal and causal chains

Based on the search results, I found information about the AQA A-Level Punjabi specification 7682 subject content themes. Here's what the specification includes:

## Main Themes

The A-level Punjabi 7682 specification covers:
1. Social issues and trends, past and present
2. Political and artistic culture, past and present

## Detailed Sub-themes

One key theme is "Aspects of Panjabi-speaking society: past and current" which includes reasons for migration and advantages and disadvantages for the Punjab.

Another theme is "Artistic culture in the Panjabi-speaking world past and present" which covers aspects such as roots and origins, and social and economic impact.

## Research Topics

Students must choose one of the research topics which include: The changing role of women in society, Crime and its consequences for individuals and society, Impact of poverty on society, The development of a tourist infrastructure, and Background to the Partition.

The specification requires students to study the themes and sub-themes in relation to the Punjab, using a range of sources, including material from online media.

# AQA A-Level Panjabi 7682 Assessment Papers

## Paper 1: Reading and Writing
- **Duration:** 2 hours 30 minutes
- **Total marks:** 85
- **Weighting:** 42.5% of A-level
- **Format:** Written exam
- **Content assessed:** Social issues and trends (past/current), political and artistic culture, grammar, individual research project
- **Materials allowed:** No dictionary access
- **Question breakdown:**
  - Reading comprehension with non-verbal or Panjabi responses: 35 marks
  - Translation into English (minimum 100 words): 10 marks
  - Individual research project essay (approximately 300 words): 40 marks

## Paper 2: Writing
- **Duration:** 2 hours
- **Total marks:** 80
- **Weighting:** 20% of A-level
- **Format:** Written exam
- **Content assessed:** One text and one film OR two texts; grammar and critical analysis
- **Materials allowed:** No text, film, or dictionary access
- **Question format:** Essays requiring critical appreciation (approximately 300 words each)

## Paper 3: Listening, Reading and Writing
- **Duration:** 2 hours 30 minutes
- **Total marks:** 75
- **Weighting:** 37.5% of A-level
- **Format:** Written exam with studio recordings
- **Content assessed:** Social issues, political/artistic culture, grammar
- **Materials allowed:** No dictionary access
- **Question breakdown:**
  - Listening comprehension: 35 marks
  - Translation into Panjabi (minimum 100 words): 10 marks
  - Multi-skill task essay (approximately 200 words): 30 marks

# AQA A-Level Panjabi 7682 Research Topics

Students must select one of four research topics and cover all associated bullet points:

## 1. The role of women in Panjabi society
- "The changing role of women in society"
- "The role of women in the family"
- How employed women influence the broader Panjabi community

## 2. Social issues in the Punjab
- Criminal activity and its effects on individuals and communities
- "Impact of poverty on society"
- Approaches to addressing societal challenges

## 3. Tourism in the Punjab
- Development of tourism facilities and infrastructure
- "Popular tourist sites/places of interest"
- Regional food and culinary traditions

## 4. Partition of the Punjab in 1947
- Historical circumstances preceding the Partition
- "Events of the Partition"
- How the 1947 division continues affecting contemporary society

Students must gather relevant Panjabi-language sources to conduct independent research, demonstrating their ability to analyze and synthesize findings in the research project essay submitted for Paper 1 assessment.

> AGENT

Doc lives at `docs/exam-prep-research.md`. Here's the strategic summary so it's all in one place:

## The market gap is real

**There is no online prep platform for GCSE or A-Level Panjabi.** UK supplementary schools use the JS Nagra books + photocopied past papers. Heritage families pay £15–40/hr for iTalki tutors. That's the entire market.

## What the three books are actually for

| Book | Maps to | What it teaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Book 1** (49 pp) | Already in akhar | Script — alphabet, vowels, diacritics |
| **Book 2** (69 pp) | Future feature | Beginner readers — character-driven narratives (Manpreet, Gurpal, Charanjit...) with comprehension Qs + mirror tasks |
| **Book 3** (93 pp) | Future feature | Intermediate readers — longer narratives + animal fables (greedy dog, meeting of mice) |

The format we'd steal: every lesson ends with **"Like Manpreet, write 10 sentences about yourself."** Mirror tasks force productive output, which is exactly what GCSE Papers 2 + 4 (Speaking + Writing) test.

## GCSE Panjabi (AQA 8683)

- **4 papers** × 25% each: Listening (35–45 min), Speaking (NEA, 7–12 min), Reading (45–60 min, includes PA→EN translation), Writing (1–1h15, includes EN→PA translation)
- **Foundation tier** (grades 1–5) or **Higher tier** (grades 4–9)
- **3 themes / 12 topics** — family, tech, free time, customs, town, social issues, global issues, travel, studies, school, post-16, jobs
- **Full grammar list** captured in the doc (subjunctive, imperatives, participles, future, passives, postpositions, conditionals, etc.)

## A-Level Panjabi (AQA 7682)

- **3 papers**: Reading+Writing (42.5%), literary essays (20%), Listening+Reading+Writing (37.5%)
- **5 prescribed texts/films**: *Noori* (B.S. Shaad), *Ristian de Rang* (G.S. Bainiwal), *Savee Pattar* (M. Singh), *Asa Nu Maan Watna Da* (2004), *Jatt and Juliet 2* (2013)
- **4 research topics**: women's role / social issues / tourism / Partition 1947
- **No dictionaries** in any paper. **300-word essays.**

## Positioning + monetisation

| Tier | Price | What's in it |
|---|---|---|
| **Free** | £0 | Everything we have today: alphabet curriculum + sakhi reader |
| **akhar Pro** | £8–12/mo | GCSE topic packs, writing/translation drills with AI marking, past-paper practice, unlimited SRS, progress tracking |
| **akhar A-Level** | £15–20/mo or £150/yr | Annotated prescribed-text readers, film transcripts, research-topic Panjabi-language source library, essay marking |

**The killer feature**: AQA-rubric-aligned AI marking of writing + translation answers. Feed student response + AQA mark scheme to an LLM, return scored rubric breakdown + error highlights + suggested rewrites. Replaces the most mechanical (and expensive) part of private tutoring.

## Recommended build order from here

1. **SRS review UI** — cards already save to Supabase via the deck button, but there's no review flow yet. Smallest gap to close, biggest learning-platform unlock.
2. **GCSE topic packs** — start with Theme 1 Topic 1 (Me, family, friends). Vocab + example sentences, AQA-aligned.
3. **Reading lessons** — Book 2/3 format, our own narratives written around GCSE themes.
4. **Writing drills with AI marking** — the killer feature, ships the Pro tier.
5. **Translation drills** — both directions, auto-marked.
6. **Listening practice** — convert reading lessons to audio + comprehension Qs (we already have the TTS).
7. **A-Level tier** — annotated texts/films + research source library.

Sources:
- [JS Nagra, Panjabi Made Easy Book 1](https://archive.org/details/PanjabiMadeEasy-Book1)
- [JS Nagra, Panjabi Made Easy Book 2](https://archive.org/details/PanjabiMadeEasy-Book2)
- [JS Nagra, Panjabi Made Easy Book 3](https://archive.org/details/PanjabiMadeEasy-Book3)
- [AQA GCSE Panjabi 8683 specification](https://www.aqa.org.uk/subjects/panjabi/gcse/panjabi-8683/specification)
- [AQA A-Level Panjabi 7682 specification](https://www.aqa.org.uk/subjects/panjabi/a-level/panjabi-7682/specification)

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive review and comparison of the best Punjabi learning apps in 2026:

## Top Punjabi Learning Apps in 2026

### **1. Preply**
Preply is the category-leading and largest online tutoring marketplace that offers customized 1-on-1 Punjabi lessons online with native tutors, connecting learners from 180 countries with a global network of more than 100,000 tutors teaching over 90 languages. Preply asks you about your goals, proficiency, and availability to match you with the right tutors.

### **2. Ling App**
The Ling app offers a variety of fun mini-games and exercises designed to level up your reading and listening skills while expanding your vocabulary, with activities such as fill-in-the-blank and multiple-choice exercises complemented by interactive chatbots.

### **3. Pimsleur**
The Pimsleur app focuses on teaching Punjabi through 30-minute audio lessons that enhance your listening and speaking abilities, led by an English-speaking guide that breaks down the grammar and phrases used in everyday Punjabi conversations. Pimsleur Punjabi costs $19.95/month for app access or $150 for a complete level purchase, and the platform offers a 7-day free trial period.

### **4. Mango Languages**
Mango Languages probably has one of the most thorough Punjabi courses out of all the other language-learning apps, emphasizing every part of the language, from vocabulary to grammar to listening and speaking skills.

### **5. Language Curry**
Language Curry teaches you Punjabi words, phrases, and sentences through gamified learning, organizing vocabulary into common themes like Punjabi greetings, food, travel, and daily activities, with flashcards that include audio recordings from native speakers.

### **6. Mondly**
Mondly combines gamification with language learning through interactive lessons, quizzes, and virtual reality experiences, using speech recognition to evaluate pronunciation and provide instant feedback on speaking exercises. Mondly offers monthly subscriptions at $9.99/month, annual plans at $4.99/month, or lifetime access for $99.99.

### **7. uTalk**
uTalk offers brief lessons across 60+ topics, perfect for fitting language practice into a hectic schedule, allowing you to select topics to focus on and listen to audio clips from native Punjabi speakers.

Each app caters to different learning preferences—choose Preply for personalized tutoring, Ling or Mango Languages for gamified learning, Pimsleur for audio-focused instruction, or Mondly for VR-enhanced experiences.

## Global Punjabi Speakers

Punjabi is spoken by around 150 million people worldwide, making it one of the most widely spoken languages in the world.

## South Asia

In Pakistan, ethnic Punjabis number approximately 112.8 million with an estimated national population of 252 million in 2024. Punjabis comprise 2.7% (38,046,464) of India's total population of 1,409,128,296 per 2024 estimate by the World Factbook.

## Diaspora Populations

The Punjabi diaspora numbers around the world has been given between 3 and 5 million, mainly concentrated in Britain, Canada, the United States, Western Europe, Southeast Asia, the Middle East, Australia and New Zealand.

Punjabi is spoken among a significant overseas diaspora, particularly in Canada, the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, and the Gulf states.

For specific country rankings:

- **Canada**: Canada has the largest Sikh population outside India, largely due to those born overseas outside Canada numbering 500,000+.

- **United Kingdom**: England ranks number 1 for having the largest number born in the diaspora.

- **Language Rankings**: Punjabi is Canada's 4th most spoken language and the 3rd most spoken language in the United Kingdom.

## Supplementary Schools and Heritage Language Education in the UK

Community-led heritage language settings include supplementary and complementary schools, as well as Saturday schools. Punjabi families abroad are eager for their children to learn to read, write and converse in their mother tongue. ## Tuition Market

Second- and third-generation diaspora kids in America, Britain, and the Gulf are desperate to keep their mother tongues alive, highlighting significant untapped market demand for heritage language education services in the UK and globally.

## Duolingo Monetization Model Overview

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of Duolingo's monetization strategy:

### Freemium Model Foundation

Duolingo operates on a freemium business model, offering core language-learning functionality at no cost while charging for premium features and experiences. The freemium strategy serves multiple purposes: it maximizes user acquisition by eliminating financial barriers to entry, builds network effects through social features, and creates a massive audience for monetization through advertising and subscriptions.

### Revenue Streams

The company generates 73% of revenue from premium subscriptions (Duolingo Super) that remove ads and add features, 15% from advertising shown to free users, and 11% from the Duolingo English Test. This freemium model converts approximately 8% of active users into paying subscribers while monetizing the remaining 92% through advertising.

### Super Duolingo Pricing Strategy

Super Duolingo (Monthly) costs approximately $12.99/month, with annual pricing at $83.99 – $95.99/year (approximately $6.99 – $7.99/month), and a Family Plan available for $119.99/year covering up to 6 users. Duolingo Max (AI-Enhanced) is priced at approximately $29.99/month or $168/year.

### Premium Subscription Benefits

These include ad-free learning, offline access to lessons, unlimited hearts to prevent interruptions, progress tracking, and learning insights.

### Conversion and Engagement Strategy

Users who complete lessons seven days consecutively convert to Super at rates 3-4x higher than less engaged users. Additionally, Duolingo offers a 3/7 day free trial to test their "Super Duolingo" experience and after 7 days, it downgrades to their normal experience.

### Recent Market Reception

It's worth noting that Duolingo's stock has plummeted roughly 30% as users revolt against increased ads and aggressive subscription pushes, revealing a strategy that has alienated a significant portion of its user base with more ads, more aggressive subscription pushes.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about italki and Preply's tutor marketplace models, pricing, and commission structures:

## Commission Models

italki keeps things simple with a flat 15% commission regardless of how many hours you've taught or how long you've been on the platform. In contrast, Preply takes 18–33% per lesson, using a sliding scale where the tutor is charged a percentage of the hourly rate (between 18% and 33%), with the rate depending on the total number of lesson hours a tutor has taught on the platform.

## Revenue Model Overview

Preply's main income source comes from charging tutors a percentage commission on their lesson earnings, with this commission-based approach meaning the platform only earns money when tutors successfully deliver paid lessons. Similarly, italki takes 15% flat commission, paying tutors even on discounted trials, fostering a massive supply of 10,000+ independent pros/community tutors across niches.

## Pricing Structure

italki usually has lower starting rates, especially with Community Tutors, where many lessons fall in the $4–$20/hour range. Preply tends to sit higher overall, with most tutors charging about $10–$40/hour.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding EdTech language app conversion rate benchmarks for freemium to paid subscriber models:

## Key Benchmarks

Successful EdTech platforms with mature freemium models convert between 2% and 8% of free users to paid. More specifically, Duolingo operates at approximately 8%, and most early-stage platforms target 2–4% as a viable benchmark at launch.

Another source provides slightly broader ranges: EdTech freemium conversions range between 5% and 8%, while free trials often convert at rates as high as 22%.

However, there's variation across the broader EdTech industry. Education/EdTech has the lowest average at 2.6% across all freemium models, while freemium models typically land between 2% and 5%.

## What Drives Conversion

For language apps specifically, streak mechanics with paid recovery options, AI-powered adaptive learning paths, verified certificates, and access to live instruction are the highest-converting features. Free users convert to paid when they hit one of three specific triggers: accountability structures, credential or certification value, or unlocking functionality they've become dependent on.

The variation in these benchmarks reflects differences in product maturity, user cohorts, and the specific monetization mechanics employed.

## Average Price Per Hour for GCSE Language Tutoring

Private language lessons vary, with German at £21.39 and Spanish at £18.64 per hour. More broadly, the average price of a language tutor is around £29.24 per hour, but prices can vary widely depending on your chosen language and your learning goals.

## General GCSE Tutoring Context

For GCSE tutoring more broadly, most private tutors in the UK charge between £30 and £50 per hour, with the average sitting around £35–40/hour. It's worth noting that the average hourly cost of a GCSE tutor is around £39 for face‑to‑face lessons and £31 for online sessions.

beginner-script teaching with intermediate reading + exam prep in one product\n\n**This is the gap akhar fills.** Nothing in this list is even attempting to\nbe a complete Punjabi-learning platform. Pimsleur is the strongest at audio\nbut does nothing else. Mango is the broadest but shallow on every axis.\n\n---\n\n## 3. The benchmark: how big language-learning apps work\n\n### Duolingo (the giant)\n\n- **Revenue Q3 2025**: $271.7M (41% YoY growth)\n- **MAU**: 135.3M\n- **Paid subscribers**: 11.5M\n- **Paid conversion**: 9% of LTM MAUs — best-in-class for the freemium\n  category\n- **ARPU (paid)**: ~$94/yr per paying subscriber\n- **Blended ARPU (all MAUs)**: ~$8/yr (because 91% are free)\n\n**Revenue mix:**\n- 73% premium subscriptions (Super Duolingo, Max)\n- 15% advertising (to free users)\n- 11% Duolingo English Test (certified English proficiency for university\n  admissions — a separate B2C product)\n\n**Pricing tiers:**\n- Free (ad-supported, limited hearts/lessons)\n- Super Duolingo: $12.99/mo or $83.99/yr ($7/mo annual)\n- Family Plan: $119.99/yr for 6 users\n- Duolingo Max (AI tutoring + role-play): $29.99/mo or $168/yr\n- Free 7-day trial → ~22% trial-to-paid conversion\n\n**Key levers that drove their growth from 3% to 9% conversion:**\n1. Streak mechanics (paid recovery option for broken streaks)\n2. Family plan (lifted households not individuals)\n3. Hearts system (gates progress on engagement)\n4. AI-driven adaptive paths (Max tier)\n5. Aggressive trial-to-paid funnel\n\n**Lesson for akhar**: pure-vocab gamification is Duolingo's lane. Don't\ncompete on that — we'd lose to a $1B company. **Compete on content depth +\nexam alignment + cultural authenticity**, which Duolingo is structurally\nincapable of providing for a \"small\" language like Punjabi.\n\n### Pimsleur, Babbel, Mango, LingQ, Mondly\n\n| App | Monthly | Annual | Lifetime | Model |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Pimsleur Premium | $19.95 | ~$170/yr | — | Audio courses, single language |\n| Pimsleur All Access | $20.95 | — | — | Audio courses, all 50+ languages |\n| Babbel | $13.95 | $99/yr | — | Lessons + Live tier higher |\n| Mango (single lang) | $11.99 | ~$80/yr | — | Library-distributed via Mango Libraries |\n| Mango (all langs) | $19.99 | $179/yr | — | Direct consumer |\n| LingQ | $14.99 | $107.88/yr | — | Reading-focused, content libraries |\n| Mondly | $9.99 | $59.88/yr | $99.99 | Bite-sized lessons, all languages |\n| Memrise | $8.99 | $59.99/yr | $139.99 | Community decks + official courses |\n| Drops | $9.99 | $69.99/yr | $149.99 | Image-vocab drills |\n| ELSA Speak | $11.99 | $79.99/yr | — | Pronunciation-focused, AI-assessed |\n| Speak | $19.99 | $99.99/yr | — | AI conversation tutor |\n\n**Range that works for serious language learners: £8–20/mo.** Sweet spot\nfor \"value\" pricing is ~£8/mo annual ($96/yr). Premium tier with AI\nfeatures: $20+/mo.\n\n### Tutor marketplaces\n\n| Platform | Tutor pricing | Platform take | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Preply | $10–$40/hr | 18–33% sliding | Bigger consumer brand |\n| italki | $4–$20/hr (community) / $15–$40 (pro) | 15% flat | Larger tutor base, lower friction |\n| Verbling | $15–$50/hr | 15% | Smaller, more premium tutors |\n\n**The take-rate model** (15–33% commission) is one akhar could add later if\nwe want to offer 1:1 tutor sessions on top of the self-study product.\n\n### UK private tutoring (the \"we replace this\" benchmark)\n\n- UK private tutoring market: **£2B/year** (Sutton Trust)\n- Average tutor rate: £29.24/hr for languages, £35–40/hr for GCSE\n- Online GCSE tutoring: £31/hr average\n- A GCSE student averages 20–40 hrs of tutoring across their two-year\n  course = **£800–£1,600/student**\n\nIf akhar Pro at £10/mo replaces even 1/3 of that — student saves £400+ per\nyear. Easy sell to parents.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Market sizing for akhar\n\n### TAM / SAM / SOM\n\n**TAM (Total Addressable Market)** — everyone who could conceivably use a\nPunjabi learning product, paid or free:\n\n- 5M diaspora + UK/Canada/US/Australia hobbyist learners\n- ≈ 5M people\n\n**SAM (Serviceable Addressable Market)** — diaspora + heritage segment\nwilling to pay for a digital product:\n\n- ~400–450k households globally (calculated above)\n- At ARPU $80/yr (mid-range subscription): **SAM ≈ $32–36M/year**\n\n**SOM (Serviceable Obtainable Market)** — what we could realistically\ncapture in 3–5 years as a focused product:\n\n- **Year 1**: 0.5% of SAM (2,000–2,250 paid subscribers)\n- **Year 3**: 3% of SAM (12,000–13,500 paid subscribers)\n- **Year 5**: 10% of SAM (40,000–45,000 paid subscribers)\n\n### Revenue scenarios\n\nUsing a freemium model with **6% paid conversion** (between EdTech average\n2.6% and Duolingo's 9%) and **blended ARPU £80/yr**:\n\n| Scenario | Free MAU | Paid subs | Annual revenue |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **Pessimistic** — 5k MAU, 2% conversion | 5,000 | 100 | **£8,000** |\n| **Modest** — 30k MAU, 4% conversion | 30,000 | 1,200 | **£96,000** |\n| **Plausible Y2** — 100k MAU, 5% conversion | 100,000 | 5,000 | **£400,000** |\n| **Plausible Y3** — 250k MAU, 6% conversion | 250,000 | 15,000 | **£1.2M** |\n| **Optimistic Y5** — 500k MAU, 8% conversion | 500,000 | 40,000 | **£3.2M** |\n| **Best case Y5** — 1M MAU, 9% conversion (Duolingo-level) | 1,000,000 | 90,000 | **£7.2M** |\n\nFor context: Duolingo has 135M MAUs against ~1.5B English-as-second-language\nlearners. A 0.5%-of-niche grab in Punjabi is comparable.\n\n**At \"Plausible Y3\" (£1.2M revenue)** akhar can support a real team\n(2 engineers + 1 content/curriculum lead + 1 marketer + £200k margin).\nThat's a fundable, viable business.\n\n### The exam-prep premium wedge\n\nThe 963 GCSE + 167 A-Level annual candidates are the **highest-value** part\nof SAM:\n\n- GCSE: 963 candidates × £150/yr (Pro tier 1-year sub) = **£144k/yr if\n  100% conversion** (unrealistic — at 30% capture = £43k/yr)\n- A-Level: 167 candidates × £200/yr (A-Level tier) = **£33k/yr if 100%\n  conversion** (at 30% capture = £10k/yr)\n- Plus US/Canada equivalent exams: similar order of magnitude\n\nSo exam-prep alone is a £50–100k niche — small but high-margin and\ndefensible. The real upside is using it as the **acquisition wedge**:\nparents pay because exam grades matter. Those students then continue using\nakhar past their exams, recommend it to siblings, and the heritage-learner\ntier opens up.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Monetization paths\n\n### Path A: Pure freemium subscription (Duolingo / Babbel model)\n\n- Free: alphabet curriculum + sakhi reader + limited SRS deck\n- Pro: £8/mo or £80/yr — unlimited SRS, writing drills, exam prep, audio\n  downloads\n- Family Plan: £150/yr for 5 accounts\n- Premium AI tier: £20/mo or £180/yr — AI writing marking, AI conversation\n  practice\n\n**Pros**: Recurring revenue, scales infinitely, no human-cost in delivery.\n**Cons**: Slow ramp, high churn risk, depends on engagement mechanics.\n\n### Path B: Exam prep as a discrete product\n\n- akhar GCSE Prep: £15/mo or £120/yr — full GCSE Panjabi curriculum, past\n  papers, mock exams, AI marking\n- akhar A-Level Prep: £25/mo or £200/yr — prescribed texts, film\n  transcripts, research-topic resources, essay marking\n- One-time pricing for \"single-paper crash courses\" (£30 each)\n\n**Pros**: Clear value proposition, motivated buyers, less churn (they\nbuy through to the exam date). **Cons**: Seasonal (Sept–May), small\nTAM (~1,100 candidates/year).\n\n### Path C: B2B school licensing\n\n- Sell to UK supplementary/Saturday schools at £200–500/yr per school for\n  classroom licences (up to 30 students)\n- ~50 known UK Panjabi supplementary schools (Gurdwara-affiliated,\n  community-run) = **£10–25k/yr** from this segment alone\n- Plus a handful of mainstream UK secondaries that offer Panjabi GCSE\n  (~30 schools): same scale\n\n**Pros**: Big-ticket deals, predictable renewal, high LTV per account.\n**Cons**: Long sales cycles, requires school-grade compliance (GDPR,\nsafeguarding, admin dashboards).\n\n### Path D: Marketplace + take rate\n\n- Add 1:1 tutor booking on top of self-study (italki-style)\n- Take 15–20% commission on £20–40/hr lessons\n- Best as a **complement** to subscription tier, not a primary path —\n  marketplace is hard from scratch\n\n### Path E: One-time + lifetime pricing\n\n- Lifetime: £200 once (Mondly does this at $99 lifetime)\n- Single-language book purchase: £30 per \"Made Easy\" equivalent module\n- Pro: Lowers barrier to commitment, captures gift-giving market (heritage\n  parents buying for kids)\n\n### Path F: Ads on free tier\n\n- Show ads to free users; Duolingo gets 15% revenue this way\n- For akhar's likely sub-1M MAU scale: ads make ~£1–2k/mo. Doc lives at `docs/market-research.md`. Here's the summary you actually need:

## The opportunity in three numbers

- **~400–450k addressable households** globally (diaspora families willing to pay for heritage Punjabi)
- **963 GCSE + 167 A-Level** candidates per year (UK, AQA 2024) — small but stable, no digital competition
- **£2B/yr** UK private tutoring market (we're a fraction of that, but a real fraction)

## The competition (one-line verdict on each)

Reviewed every Punjabi app: Pimsleur, Mango, Ling, Mondly, Memrise, Drops, Language Curry, uTalk, HelloTalk, eLearnPunjabi, Punjabi By Choice. Plus the tutor marketplaces (Preply, italki).

**Nobody does script teaching + reading practice + exam prep + AI marking in one product.** Every existing app is either:
- Audio-only (Pimsleur)
- Generic phrase drills (Mondly, Ling, Mango)
- Tutor marketplace (Preply, italki)
- Religious/donation-funded (Punjabi By Choice)
- Government-funded but dated (eLearnPunjabi)

The gap is real and structural — Duolingo won't enter this market because it's too small for them.

## Benchmark pricing (so we know where to land)

| App | Monthly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| Babbel | $13.95 | $99 |
| LingQ | $14.99 | $108 |
| Mango (single) | $11.99 | $80 |
| Memrise | $8.99 | $60 |
| Mondly | $9.99 | $60 |
| Pimsleur | $19.95 | $170 |
| Speak (AI tier) | $19.99 | $100 |
| Duolingo Super | $12.99 | $84 |
| Duolingo Max (AI) | $29.99 | $168 |

**Sweet spot: £8/mo annual (£80/yr) for the standard tier, £20/mo for AI-enhanced.**

## Realistic revenue scenarios

Conservative 6% conversion, blended ARPU £80/yr:

| Scenario | MAUs | Paid subs | Annual revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year 1 modest | 30k | 1,200 | **£96k** |
| Year 3 plausible | 250k | 15,000 | **£1.2M** ← supports a real team |
| Year 5 optimistic | 500k | 40,000 | **£3.2M** |
| Year 5 best case (Duolingo-level penetration) | 1M | 90,000 | **£7.2M** |

For context: Duolingo gets 9% conversion at $94/yr ARPU. Our model bakes in worse-than-Duolingo on both axes and still pencils to a real business.

## Recommended monetization stack

| Tier | Price | Who |
|---|---|---|
| **Free** | £0 | Everyone — alphabet, sakhi reader (current product) |
| **akhar Pro** | £8/mo or £80/yr | Heritage learners, casual students |
| **akhar GCSE Prep** | £15/mo or £120/yr | Exam-aligned content + AI writing/translation marking |
| **(Later) A-Level** | £25/mo or £200/yr | Prescribed texts + film transcripts + essay marking |
| **(Year 2) School licensing** | £200–500/yr per school | UK supplementary/Saturday schools, ~50 known |

**The killer feature**: AQA-rubric-aligned AI marking. Saves parents £400–800/yr per child in private tutor fees. Clear ROI, easy sell.

## What to copy from others

- **Daily streak + push notifications** (Duolingo) — proven retention
- **Family Plan** (Duolingo) — perfect for heritage market (parents buying for kids)
- **7-day free trial** (everyone) — 22% trial-to-paid conversion benchmark
- **Reading + vocab tracker** (LingQ) — already our core mechanic, just need the "known words" UI
- **Listen-only mode** (Pimsleur) — commute use case, we already have the audio
- **FSRS spaced repetition** (Anki) — review UI gap to close on the existing srs_cards table

  "content": "# Content architecture\n\nHow akhar's content is organised, and how the sakhi corpus interlocks with\nGCSE/A-Level learning. This is the doc that answers: *\"what is this thing,\nactually?\"*\n\n---\n\n## The core insight\n\n**akhar has two wings on a shared foundation.** They share infrastructure\n(script, dictionary, audio, deck, account) but serve different needs and\nshould look like different products in the navigation.\n\n```\n                         ┌─────────────────────┐\n                         │     ALPHABET        │\n                         │  (script learning)  │\n                         │   58 lessons        │\n                         │   Already built     │\n                         └──────────┬──────────┘\n                                    │\n                ┌───────────────────┴───────────────────┐\n                │                                       │\n                ▼                                       ▼\n   ┌────────────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────────┐\n   │   READ                 │            │   LEARN                  │\n   │   (the library)        │            │   (the curriculum)       │\n   │                        │            │                          │\n   │ • 405 sakhis           │            │ • Beginner readers       │\n   │ • Classical Punjabi    │            │ • GCSE topic packs       │\n   │ • Hover lookups        │            │ • Reading practice       │\n   │ • Sentence audio       │            │ • Writing + AI marking   │\n   │ • Save to deck         │            │ • Translation drills     │\n   │                        │            │ • Listening practice     │\n   │ Browse:                │            │ • Past papers + mocks    │\n   │   - by Guru            │            │ • A-Level tier:          │\n   │   - by theme           │            │   prescribed texts,      │\n   │   - by difficulty      │            │   films, research topics │\n   │   - daily pick         │            │                          │\n   └───────────┬────────────┘            └──────────────┬───────────┘\n               │                                        │\n               └────────────────┬───────────────────────┘\n                                ▼\n                  ┌──────────────────────────────┐\n                  │   SHARED INFRASTRUCTURE      │\n                  │                              │\n                  │ • Personal vocab deck (SRS)  │\n                  │ • Reading history            │\n                  │ • Streak + progress          │\n                  │ • Account + family plan      │\n                  │ • Dictionary + morpheme      │\n                  │ • Chirp 3 TTS audio cache    │\n                  └──────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n**Read** is the literature library — sakhis. **Learn** is the structured\ncurriculum — alphabet, beginner readers, GCSE, A-Level. They cross-link in\nspecific places but they are not the same product surface.\n\n---\n\n## Why this split (the honest version)\n\nA sakhi is not a GCSE text. GCSE tests modern conversational Punjabi about\nfamily, school, technology, environment, jobs. Sakhis are 19th/20th-century\nliterary prose about Sikh Gurus. The diction, register, vocabulary, and\ngrammar all differ.\n\nIf we tried to fold sakhis into GCSE prep, we'd confuse beginners and\nmislead exam candidates. If we tried to make sakhis the \"advanced\" tier\nabove GCSE, we'd hide the spiritually/culturally valuable content from\nthe audience that most wants it (heritage learners who already have some\nPunjabi but don't speak it well).\n\n**Both wings stand alone** — a heritage parent might never touch GCSE prep\nbut will pay £8/mo to read sakhis with hover-translation. A GCSE student\nmight never finish a sakhi but will pay £15/mo for AI-marked writing\npractice. Different people, different journeys, same platform.\n\n---\n\n## How the sakhi corpus gets dished out\n\nWe have 405 sakhis from 5 books across 10 Gurus. Currently 1 is fully\nprocessed (sakhi 1, \"Our handsome Guru's house\"). The processing pipeline\nexists (corpus/ folder + Processing.md). The architectural question is:\n**how does a user find the right next sakhi to read?**\n\n### Browse modes (`/sakhis`)\n\n| Mode | What it does | Who it serves |\n|---|---|---|\n| **By Guru** | The current `/guru/[id]` listing — sakhis grouped by which Guru's life they cover | Devotional readers, traditional study |\n| **By book** | Each of the 5 source books as a coherent reading order | Followers of a specific author (e.g., all of Bhai Vir Singh's Gur Balam Sakhian) |\n| **By difficulty** | Auto-scored 1-5 stars based on sentence length, vocab complexity, archaic terms count | Learners progressing |\n| **By theme tag** | childhood / miracles / journeys / family / courage / devotion / household / nature | Topic-driven browsers |\n| **Daily sakhi** | One picked per day based on user's reading level + history | Habit-building, \"akhar of the day\" email |\n| **Continue reading** | Resume the last sakhi you opened | The default home for returning users |\n| **Bookmarks** | Sakhis you've saved | Personal library |\n| **Random surprise** | \"I'm feeling lucky\" button | Discovery |\n\nThe default landing should be **continue + recommended** rather than the\nfull library — too overwhelming otherwise. The full library is a\nsecondary tab.\n\n### Within a sakhi\n\nThe reader stays as we've built it: parallel text, hover translations,\nsentence audio. Additions to make:\n\n- **Reading streak**: each sakhi finished counts toward a daily/weekly\n  streak (cf. Duolingo)\n- **Words learnt counter**: as you hover-lookup new words, increment a\n  \"you've encountered N new words in this sakhi\" counter\n- **One-tap-to-deck**: keep the existing Save button\n- **Mark complete**: explicit button at the end → unlocks progress display\n- **Bookmark a paragraph**: come back to where you stopped\n- **Notes**: per-paragraph user notes (paid feature)\n\n### Recommendations across the corpus\n\nOnce enough sakhis are processed, the recommendation engine can:\n\n- \"You just finished a story about Guru Nanak's childhood — try this one\n  about Guru Angad's childhood (related theme + similar difficulty)\"\n- \"You know 75% of the vocabulary in this sakhi — easy read, try it\"\n- \"You haven't read anything from Guru Hargobind — start here\"\n\nDoesn't need ML — a simple Postgres query over tags + difficulty + your\nknown-words count gets you 90% of the way.\n\n---\n\n## How the curriculum (GCSE/A-Level) gets dished out\n\nGCSE Panjabi is structured by AQA's spec: 3 themes, 12 topics. A-Level\nadds prescribed texts + films + research topics. We mirror that\nstructure on the surface.\n\n### The Learn track (`/learn`)\n\n```\n/learn                                       — entry, shows your path + progress\n├── /learn/alphabet                          — already exists, the 58 lessons\n├── /learn/beginner                          — Book 2/3 style readers (NEW)\n│     ├── /learn/beginner/01-introductions\n│     ├── /learn/beginner/02-family\n│     ├── /learn/beginner/03-school\n│     ├── /learn/beginner/04-daily-routine\n│     └── ...\n├── /learn/gcse                              — GCSE Panjabi 8683\n│     ├── /learn/gcse/theme/1-identity-and-culture\n│     │     ├── /learn/gcse/theme/1/topic/1-family-and-friends\n│     │     │     ├── vocabulary pack\n│     │     │     ├── reading passages\n│     │     │     ├── writing prompts\n│     │     │     ├── translation drills\n│     │     │     └── listening exercises\n│     │     ├── /learn/gcse/theme/1/topic/2-technology\n│     │     ├── /learn/gcse/theme/1/topic/3-free-time\n│     │     └── /learn/gcse/theme/1/topic/4-customs\n│     ├── /learn/gcse/theme/2-...\n│     ├── /learn/gcse/theme/3-...\n│     ├── /learn/gcse/grammar                — full grammar reference + drills\n│     └── /learn/gcse/papers                 — past papers + mock exams\n└── /learn/a-level                           — AQA 7682 (later)\n      ├── /learn/a-level/texts/noori\n      ├── /learn/a-level/texts/ristian-de-rang\n      ├── /learn/a-level/texts/savee-pattar\n      ├── /learn/a-level/films/asa-nu-maan-watna-da\n      ├── /learn/a-level/films/jatt-and-juliet-2\n      └── /learn/a-level/research/...\n```\n\n### Each topic pack has the same shape\n\nEvery GCSE topic looks like this internally:\n\n1. **Vocabulary pack** — ~40 words for the topic, with audio + example sentence\n2. **Reading passage** — 200-400 word narrative on the topic, hover-lookup, audio\n3. **Comprehension Qs** — auto-marked multi-choice + short-answer in PA\n4. **Writing prompt** — 40 word task (Foundation) / 90 word task (Higher),\n   AI-marked against the AQA rubric\n5. **Translation drill** — 5 sentences PA→EN + 5 EN→PA, auto-marked\n6. **Listening exercise** — 60-second audio (Chirp 3 from a scripted\n   dialogue), then comprehension Qs\n7. **Quick quiz** — 10 multi-choice on the topic's vocab and grammar\n\nThis is the \"lesson\" unit students complete. Marks roll up into a topic\nscore. Topic scores roll up into a theme readiness score. Theme readiness\nmaps to a \"you're ready for the GCSE [Foundation/Higher] exam at X%\"\nindicator.\n\n### Diagnostic + placement\n\nOn first visit to `/learn/gcse`:\n- \"Have you studied any Punjabi before?\" Yes/No\n- If yes: 15-minute placement quiz (reading + writing + vocab check)\n- Output: \"Start at Theme 1 Topic 2\" or \"You're ready for Higher Tier mocks\"\n- Re-takeable any time\n\n### Past papers as the capstone\n\nWe obtain publicly released AQA past papers + mark schemes (they're free\nto use under AQA's terms for non-commercial educational use — we'll need\nto verify for paid use). Students can take them under timed conditions,\nAI marks the writing/translation portions, listening uses our TTS.\n\nA-Level adds: 300-word essays on prescribed texts, AI-marked against\nmark scheme.\n\n---\n\n## How the two wings cross-link\n\nFive concrete touchpoints where the library and the curriculum talk to\neach other:\n\n1. **Shared SRS deck.** Words saved from a sakhi land in the same deck as\n   words from a GCSE topic pack. Vocabulary compounds; you're not building\n   two separate brains.\n\n2. **\"Suggested sakhi\" inside GCSE topics.** When studying *Theme 1 Topic\n   4: Customs and festivals*, the topic page recommends sakhis tagged\n   with related themes (Vaisakhi, Diwali, gurpurabs). Reading them is\n   optional but enriches the topic.\n\n3. **\"Related GCSE theme\" on sakhi pages.** When reading a sakhi about\n   family relationships, a small footer link says \"this sakhi practices\n   vocabulary used in *GCSE Theme 1 Topic 1: Family and friends*.\"\n\n4. **Shared dictionary**. Every word in every text — sakhi, beginner\n   reader, GCSE passage, A-Level text — looks up to the same morpheme\n   cache. Glosses, etymologies, audio are consistent everywhere.\n\n5. **\"Known words\" counter applies everywhere.** Your personal known-words\n   set drives recommendations across both wings: easier sakhis to read,\n   GCSE topics where you already know most of the vocab, etc.\n\n---\n\n## What the navigation looks like\n\nAfter signing in:\n\n```\n┌─ Top nav ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│  akhar     [Read] [Learn] [Deck] [Profile]      [search]   │\n└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n- **Read** — sakhi library (current /sakhi + /guru flows)\n- **Learn** — `/learn` (alphabet, beginner, GCSE, A-Level)\n- **Deck** — `/deck` SRS review (NEW, the cards table already exists)\n- **Profile** — settings, subscription, progress\n\nThe Home (`/`) for signed-in users shows:\n- \"Continue reading\" — last sakhi\n- \"Continue learning\" — next lesson in their current track\n- \"Cards due today\" — deck review prompt\n- \"Daily sakhi\" — bonus recommendation\n\nThis is more concrete than the current free-form `/` landing.\n\n---\n\n## What this means for the build\n\n**To make Read work properly we need:**\n1. Sakhi processing pipeline working at scale (more than 1/405 done)\n2. Sakhi tagging by theme + auto-difficulty scoring\n3. Browse-by-theme + recommendations UI\n4. Bookmarks + notes + \"mark complete\"\n\n**To make Learn work properly we need:**\n1. Beginner reader content (Book 2/3 equivalent — write our own narratives)\n2. GCSE topic-pack content (12 topics × the 7-part structure)\n3. Writing exercise UI + AI marking pipeline\n4. Translation drill UI + auto-marking\n5. Listening exercise UI (TTS-generated audio + comprehension Qs)\n6. Past papers — sourced + UI for timed practice\n\n**To make the cross-links work we need:**\n1. Sakhi-to-GCSE-theme tag table in Supabase\n2. Recommendations endpoint (Postgres-only — no ML needed for v1)\n3. Shared SRS deck (already done — `srs_cards` table)\n4. Known-words tracking (also already in schema — `word_encounters`)\n\nSee [build-order.md](./build-order.md) for the sequencing.\n"
}

{
  "file_path": "/Users/sumeet/matrix/web/akhar/docs/tiers.md",
  "content": "# Tiers and monetization\n\nWhat's free, what's paid, why each thing sits where it sits.\n\nThe principle: **the script and a meaningful taste of every wing are\nfree. Going deep — in either the library or the curriculum — is paid.\nAI marking and exam tooling are the premium gate.**\n\n---\n\n## The four tiers\n\n| Tier | Price | Built for |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Free** | £0 | Top of funnel — alphabet learners, casual hobbyists, \"is this app for me\" tyre-kickers |\n| **akhar Pro** | £8/mo or £80/yr | Heritage learners, serious self-study, library readers |\n| **akhar GCSE** | £15/mo or £120/yr | Active GCSE Panjabi candidates and their parents |\n| **akhar A-Level** | £25/mo or £200/yr | Active A-Level Panjabi candidates *(later phase)* |\n| Family Plan | £150/yr | Up to 5 users, Pro features. Heritage parent buying for kids. *(later phase)* |\n\nEach higher tier is a strict superset — A-Level includes everything in\nGCSE includes everything in Pro includes everything in Free.\n\n---\n\n## What's in each tier\n\n### Free (acquisition + script)\n\nThe free experience must be genuinely useful or the funnel breaks. Free\nincludes:\n\n- **Full alphabet curriculum** — all 58 lessons (paintee akhar, nukta,\n  matras, gemination, nasalisation, conjuncts, tone, stories, glossary).\n  Audio on every clip. This alone is more complete than 90% of the\n  Punjabi apps on the market.\n- **Library taster** — first 10 sakhis fully open. Hover lookups, audio,\n  save-to-deck all work. The other 395 show in the index but require Pro\n  to read.\n- **Beginner readers taster** — first 3 lessons of beginner-narrative\n  series.\n- **GCSE taster** — Theme 1 Topic 1 (Family) vocab pack + reading\n  passage. Enough to evaluate the format.\n- **SRS deck** — capped at 50 cards. Real spaced repetition works but you\n  cap out after a few sakhis.\n- **Daily streak** + push notifications + basic progress page.\n- **One device** signed in at a time. Switching is fine but no\n  simultaneous sessions.\n\nWhat's NOT free:\n- Sakhis 11–405\n- Beginner readers 4 onward\n- GCSE Theme 1 Topic 2 onward (i.e. 11 of 12 topics)\n- Writing/translation/listening exercises beyond the taster\n- AI marking of any kind\n- Audio downloads for offline use\n- Cross-device sync of bookmarks and notes\n- Family Plan\n\n### akhar Pro — £8/mo or £80/yr (heritage + self-study)\n\nThe \"I want to actually use this product\" tier. Aimed at the 400k+\nheritage-learner households globally.\n\n- Everything in Free\n- **Full sakhi library** — all 405 sakhis once processed\n- **Bookmarks, notes, mark-complete tracking** across the corpus\n- **Unlimited SRS deck**\n- **All beginner reader lessons** (the full Book 2/3 equivalent\n  curriculum — modern Punjabi narratives we author ourselves)\n- **All GCSE topic packs (vocab + reading components only)** — vocabulary\n  + reading passages + comprehension Qs for all 12 topics, all 3 themes.\n  Listening and writing/translation/AI marking are gated to GCSE tier.\n- **Audio downloads for offline** — PWA cache so you can read on a\n  flight. Big selling point for diaspora.\n- **Cross-device sync** — sign in on phone, laptop, iPad; bookmarks +\n  deck + progress travel with you.\n- **Custom decks** — group saved words into themed decks (\"words from\n  Guru Nanak sakhis\", \"vocab from Jasveer's family lesson\")\n- **Reading goals + analytics** — set a daily word/sakhi target, see\n  weekly recap email, \"you read X sakhis and learnt Y words this month\"\n\nNot in Pro:\n- AI marking\n- Translation drills\n- Writing exercise UI\n- Listening exercises beyond the topic-pack tasters\n- Past papers\n- Mock exams\n- A-Level content\n\n### akhar GCSE — £15/mo or £120/yr (exam prep)\n\nThe exam-prep killer feature tier. The reason a parent pays this is\nbecause **AI marking saves them £400+/yr in private tutor fees**.\n\n- Everything in Pro\n- **AI-marked writing exercises** — every topic pack's writing prompts\n  (40-word message, 90-word structured task, 150-word open-ended) get\n  marked by an LLM against the actual AQA mark scheme. Returns:\n    - Rubric-aligned score (Content + Range and Accuracy of Language)\n    - Highlighted errors with explanations\n    - Suggested rewrites\n    - Foundation vs Higher tier specific feedback\n- **AI-marked translation drills** — both PA→EN and EN→PA, every topic\n  has a translation set. AI compares your translation against a model\n  answer, highlights deviations, scores per the AQA scheme.\n- **Listening exercises** — 60s scripted dialogues (TTS'd via Chirp 3)\n  with comprehension questions. Covers the Paper 1 Listening format\n  for both tiers.\n- **Past papers + mark schemes** — every released AQA past paper since\n  the spec started (2017+), under timed conditions. AI marks the\n  open-ended portions; multi-choice and matching are auto-marked.\n- **Mock exam mode** — full timed simulation of all four GCSE papers,\n  with the same time/marks/format as the real thing.\n- **Speaking prep** — role-play scripts, photo-card prompts, general\n  conversation question banks. NOTE: actual voice scoring is a\n  follow-on feature; for v1, students record themselves and self-rate\n  against the rubric.\n- **Grammar drills** — per-tense, per-construction practice (every item\n  in the AQA grammar list — subjunctive, imperative, passive, etc. —\n  gets its own drill set).\n- **Progress dashboard** with AQA-style \"predicted grade\" based on\n  marked output.\n\nSpecifically priced for the GCSE candidate market — 963 UK candidates a\nyear, average £400/yr saved on tutoring = strong value.\n\n### akhar A-Level — £25/mo or £200/yr (deferred phase 2)\n\nFor the 167 UK A-Level candidates a year + international.\n\n- Everything in GCSE\n- **Annotated readers for prescribed texts** — Noori (Boota Singh Shaad),\n  Ristian de Rang (Gurmel Singh Bainiwal), Savee Pattar (Mohan Singh).\n  Each text segmented chapter-by-chapter with:\n    - Full text with hover-translation (same reader as sakhis)\n    - Critical notes per chapter\n    - Themes + character analysis\n    - Sample essay outlines\n- **Annotated film transcripts** — Asa Nu Maan Watna Da (2004), Jatt and\n  Juliet 2 (2013). Scene-by-scene transcripts with translation, themes,\n  cinematography notes.\n- **Research-topic library** — curated Panjabi-language source material\n  for each of the 4 research topics (women's role, social issues,\n  tourism, Partition 1947): news articles, podcasts, academic excerpts,\n  vocabulary glossaries.\n- **Essay marking** — 300-word essays on prescribed texts, marked\n  against AQA's literary mark scheme.\n- **Research project tracker** — guided workflow for the\n  individual-research-project component of Paper 1.\n\nBuilt later. Lower MAU, higher ARPU, harder content to produce\n(requires partnerships or commissioned writing).\n\n### Family Plan — £150/yr (heritage parent dream)\n\nSame features as Pro tier but for up to 5 users. Built once Pro has\nvolume. The mechanism:\n\n- One billing account, 5 separate profiles with own progress/decks\n- Family-only leaderboard (\"Mum's read 12 sakhis this month, you're at\n  3\")\n- Per-child age-appropriate recommendations\n- Designed for households where a parent wants the whole family\n  engaging with Punjabi\n\nFamily Plan customers convert at ~3x baseline (Duolingo's data) and have\n~5x LTV because of the household lock-in.\n\n---\n\n## What's NOT gated even at premium tiers\n\nThings that stay free for everyone, even at A-Level tier:\n\n- **The alphabet curriculum** — script learning is the gift to the\n  community, never paywall it\n- **Public landing pages, SEO content, sample lessons** — top of funnel\n- **The dictionary itself** — `/api/morpheme` for any word should remain\n  publicly accessible. Word lookups are not the moat; the structured\n  curriculum and AI marking are.\n\n---\n\n## Trial mechanics\n\nStandard SaaS approach:\n\n- **7-day free trial of any paid tier** — credit card required upfront\n  (this filters serious vs casual). Industry benchmark: 22% trial→paid\n  conversion.\n- **Tier upgrade trials** — already on Pro? Try GCSE free for 3 days.\n- **Annual discount** — annual plans give ~16% off vs monthly\n  (£80/yr vs £96 if paid monthly).\n- **Student discount** — 50% off GCSE/A-Level tiers with proof of\n  enrolment (UCAS/UK school email). Drives GCSE tier adoption since\n  most candidates ARE students.\n\n---\n\n## How decisions get made on what to gate\n\nA simple rule: **if it costs us per-use, it goes behind a paid tier**.\n\n- LLM marking → costs us tokens → paid\n- Whisper transcription for speaking → paid\n- R2 bandwidth for audio downloads → paid (big users only)\n- Read-only access to text → free (negligible cost)\n- Hover translation → free (cached, near-zero marginal cost)\n- TTS audio playback → free (cached forever, near-zero marginal cost\n  once generated)\n\nCost-driven gating means the free tier is actually sustainable. Even at\nmassive scale, the free experience costs us almost nothing per user.\n\n---\n\n## Pricing psychology\n\n- **£8/mo** for Pro — sits below Babbel ($14), Mango ($12), Pimsleur\n  ($20). Anchors as \"obviously fair value.\"\n- **£15/mo** for GCSE — sits at the upper end of language apps but\n  cheaper than a single hour with a tutor (£30+/hr). Easy parent-budget\n  decision.\n- **£25/mo** for A-Level — still cheaper than one tutor hour, justified\n  by curated prescribed-text content nobody else provides.\n- Annual pricing always shown alongside monthly: **\"£80/yr (£6.66/mo) vs\n  £8/mo\"** — the per-month framing makes the annual look like 20% off.\n- **No lifetime tier yet** — Mondly does this at $99 lifetime, but\n  lifetimes cap LTV. Skip until growth stalls.\n\n---\n\n## What we don't do\n\n- **No ads** anywhere, ever. Duolingo's stock dropped 30% in 2025 from\n  ad-aggression backlash. Heritage parents will pay; we don't need ads.\n- **No \"buy hearts to continue\" mobile-game mechanics**. Duolingo's\n  weakest engagement lever, alienates serious learners.\n- **No crypto / NFTs / token gimmicks.**\n- **No certificate sales** unless they're genuinely recognised (Duolingo\n  English Test took years to get any accreditation — not worth it for us\n  unless we partner with an exam board).\n- **No tutor-marketplace commission as primary revenue** — wait until\n  subscription base is solid, then add it as a complement (italki-style\n  15% take).\n\n---\n\n## Free → Pro → GCSE conversion funnel\n\nThe implied funnel, with rough benchmarks:\n\n```\n100,000 free signups            (signups from SEO + diaspora marketing)\n  ├─ 6,000 → Pro                (6% Free→Pro, in line with EdTech avg)\n  │    ├─ 1,200 → GCSE          (20% Pro→GCSE — only relevant to candidates)\n  │    └─ 4,800 stay on Pro\n  └─ 94,000 stay free           (still get value, drive referrals)\n\nRevenue from this funnel:\n  4,800 Pro × £80/yr = £384k\n  1,200 GCSE × £120/yr = £144k\n  Total: £528k/yr\n```\n\nThat's the \"Plausible Y2\" scenario from market-research.md. Aim for\n100k MAU within 18 months of launch.\n\n---\n\n## See also\n\n- [content-architecture.md](./content-architecture.md) — how the content\n  itself is shaped\n- [build-order.md](./build-order.md) — when these tiers get built\n- [market-research.md](./market-research.md) — the numbers behind the\n  pricing decisions\n- [exam-prep-research.md](./exam-prep-research.md) — full AQA spec\n  details that the GCSE/A-Level tiers must satisfy\n"
}

{
  "file_path": "/Users/sumeet/matrix/web/akhar/docs/build-order.md",
  "content": "# Build order\n\nWhat we build, in what order, and why. Each phase has a clear shippable\ngoal so we can stop and validate before committing more time.\n\nThe principle: **launch the free tier first, prove people use it, then\nturn on Pro, then build GCSE features against real user demand.** Don't\nbuild the GCSE AI marker before we know if anyone wants akhar at all.\n\n---\n\n## Where we are right now (status snapshot)\n\nAlready shipped to `dev` branch:\n\n- ✅ Alphabet curriculum — 58 lessons, audio, glossary, recognition\n  exercise\n- ✅ Sakhi reader — hover popups, sentence audio, save-to-deck\n- ✅ Supabase auth (magic links), RLS, per-user data tables\n- ✅ Landing page + site header\n- ✅ Dev/main branching + Vercel preview deploys\n- ✅ R2 audio storage + Chirp 3 TTS prewarm pipeline\n- ✅ Save-to-deck button (writes to `srs_cards` table)\n\nNot yet shipped:\n\n- ⏳ Mobile-responsive pass\n- ⏳ Sakhi processing pipeline running at scale (1/405 done)\n- ⏳ SRS review UI (cards in DB, no review flow)\n- ⏳ Library browse (sakhis only listed by Guru, no theme/difficulty)\n- ⏳ Onboarding flow\n- ⏳ Pricing page + Stripe\n- ⏳ Any GCSE-specific content\n- ⏳ akhar.io DNS (still on Vercel preview URL)\n\n---\n\n## Phase 0 — Polish and launch (free tier only)\n\n**Goal: akhar.io live with the existing product, anonymous + signed-in\nusers can use everything we've built. > AGENT

Three docs pushed to `dev`. Here are the punchlines from each so you don't have to read all 900 lines unless you want to:

## `docs/content-architecture.md` — what is this thing?

**akhar = two wings on one foundation.**

- **Foundation**: the alphabet curriculum (already built). Script-learning is the universal entry point.
- **Wing 1 — Read**: the sakhi library. Classical Punjabi, 405 stories, hover-translation, audio. For heritage/devotional readers.
- **Wing 2 — Learn**: alphabet + beginner readers + GCSE topic packs + A-Level (later). Modern Punjabi, structured curriculum, exam-aligned.

They're **different products in the same app**. Top nav after sign-in: **Read · Learn · Deck · Profile**.

**Why two wings, not one funnel**: sakhis are classical literary prose; GCSE tests modern conversational Punjabi about family/school/jobs. Folding them confuses both audiences. Keeping them separate lets a heritage parent never touch GCSE and a GCSE student never read a sakhi — yet they're paying for the same product.

**How the sakhi corpus gets dished out**: browse by Guru / book / theme / difficulty + daily pick + continue reading + bookmarks. Not the full 405 in a list — that's overwhelming. Default home = "continue + recommended."

**How the wings cross-link**: shared SRS deck, shared dictionary, "suggested sakhi for this GCSE topic" pointers, and a `word_encounters` counter that flows both ways. So vocabulary learnt in one wing makes recommendations smarter in the other.

## `docs/tiers.md` — what's free, what's paid

| Tier | Price | What you get that the tier below doesn't |
|---|---|---|
| **Free** | £0 | Alphabet + 10-sakhi taster + GCSE Theme 1 Topic 1 taster + 50-card deck. Genuinely useful (more complete than 90% of Punjabi apps) — drives signups. |
| **akhar Pro** | £8/mo or £80/yr | Full 405 sakhi library, unlimited deck, all beginner readers, **GCSE vocab + reading components** (not writing/AI marking), audio downloads, cross-device sync |
| **akhar GCSE** | £15/mo or £120/yr | AI-marked writing & translation against AQA rubrics, listening exercises, past papers, mock exams, grammar drills. **The killer tier.** Saves parents £400+/yr in tutor fees. |
| **akhar A-Level** | £25/mo or £200/yr | (Later phase) Annotated *Noori* / *Ristian de Rang* / *Savee Pattar*, film transcripts, research-topic source library, essay marking |
| **Family Plan** | £150/yr | (Later phase) 5 users on Pro features. Heritage-parent killer. |

**Gating rule**: if it costs us per-use (LLM tokens, Whisper, heavy bandwidth) → paid. If it's cached / free at scale (text reads, hover lookups, played audio) → free forever. Means the free tier is actually sustainable at any scale.

**Explicitly NOT building**: ads, hearts/lives, certificates, VR, sacred-text monetization. Avoiding Duolingo's worst mistakes.

## `docs/build-order.md` — what we build, in what order

Eight phases, each with a shippable goal:

| Phase | Goal | Estimate |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Mobile pass, onboarding, bookmarks, akhar.io DNS, Capacitor submission. **Free tier live.** | 2 wks |
| **1** | SRS review UI, process 50+ sakhis (LLM-assisted), tagging, recommendations | 3 wks |
| **2** | Stripe, tier gating, free trial, audio downloads. **Pro tier live.** | 2 wks |
| **3** | Beginner readers + ONE GCSE topic pack proving the format end-to-end | 4 wks |
| **4** | AI marking pipeline. **GCSE tier live — the moment akhar becomes real exam prep.** | 3 wks |
| **5** | Remaining 11 GCSE topic packs + past papers + mock exams | 4 wks |
| **6** | Native mobile polish + Family Plan | 3 wks |
| **7** | A-Level tier (prescribed texts, films, research) | 6+ wks |
| **8+** | Speaking + AI tutor + B2B schools + other languages | Later |

**Total to "complete GCSE prep product"**: ~21 weeks (~5 months) from now if focused. Revenue from Pro starts at end of Phase 2 (~7 weeks in). Revenue from GCSE tier starts at end of Phase 4 (~14 weeks in).

The build order is opinionated but not rigid — when we get real users we adjust based on data, not vibes.

> AGENT

Honest opinion: **I'd push back on "limited free that forces upgrades."** Not because forcing upgrades is wrong in general — it's because it's wrong *for akhar specifically*. Let me explain, then propose a tight MVP.

## Why I'd avoid a hard paywall

Three things specific to akhar:

**1. Tiny addressable market.** We're chasing ~400k households globally, not millions. Every visitor who bounces because the free tier feels stingy is one we'll never get back — there's no SEO long tail of "Punjabi learning app" searches refilling the funnel like there is for "Spanish learning app." Generosity now compounds.

**2. Zero brand recognition.** Pimsleur and Babbel can afford hard paywalls because everyone already knows their name. We're starting cold — people need to discover akhar exists, try it, talk about it, share it with their kids' Saturday school WhatsApp group. None of that happens if the first thing they hit is a paywall.

**3. Heritage learning is emotional, not transactional.** Punjabi diaspora parents don't convert because a paywall forced them; they convert because they fell in love with watching their kid read ਘੋੜਾ for the first time. That feeling needs space to develop — usually a week or two of free use.

**The counterexample to study is Pimsleur**. Audio-only, hard paywall after free trial, 90-day money-back guarantee. They have ~$100M/yr revenue at high ARPU but their *growth* is anaemic because there's no viral loop. Duolingo at $271M/quarter with 135M MAUs is the alternative — generous free + ads + Pro upgrade. Different scale entirely.

For akhar's stage, **Duolingo's playbook fits, not Pimsleur's** — even though our ARPU target is higher than Duolingo's.

## What I would do instead

**Generous free tier for the foundational stuff** (alphabet, dictionary, a meaningful taste of the library) → **clear paid value for depth + convenience + AI**. Free should feel sustainable to someone who never pays; paid should feel like an obvious upgrade once they're hooked.

Specifically:
- Free **must** stay generous for the *script + dictionary* layer — that's the SEO and word-of-mouth engine. Gating "how do I read ਘੋੜਾ?" is suicidal for our funnel.
- Pro can comfortably gate the *library depth*, *deck depth*, *audio downloads*, *cross-device sync*. These are clearly "I'm serious now" features.
- GCSE tier should gate the things with real per-use cost (LLM marking) — those are also the things people pay tutors £30/hr to get.

## My MVP proposal

Cut everything not on this list. Ship in 6–8 weeks. Validate the core hypothesis: *"heritage Punjabi learners will pay £8/mo for a thoughtfully built reader."* Don't validate the GCSE thesis yet — that's MVP+1.

### MVP Free tier
- **Full alphabet curriculum** — already built. 58 lessons, audio, glossary.
- **5 sakhis** fully open with all features (hover, audio, save-to-deck). Reduce from my earlier "10" — that's enough to fall in love.
- **SRS deck capped at 100 cards** — enough to develop the habit, not enough to never need Pro.
- **No cross-device sync** — sign in on one device.
- **No audio downloads** — streaming only.

### MVP Pro tier — £8/mo or £80/yr
- Everything in Free
- **All 50+ processed sakhis** (target for MVP: ~50 sakhis processed via LLM-assisted pipeline)
- **Unlimited deck**
- **Cross-device sync**
- **Audio downloads (PWA offline cache)**
- **Reading goals + streak tracking**

### What's NOT in MVP (defer to post-launch)
- GCSE tier (build only after Pro has paying users)
- AI marking (the killer feature, but expensive to build right — wait for revenue to justify)
- A-Level tier
- Beginner readers (the Book 2/3 stuff — build only if MVP validates and we need more depth)
- Native iOS/Android apps (web + PWA is enough — Capacitor wrap as Phase 2)
- Family Plan (build when we have ≥1,000 Pro users)
- Topic packs / writing drills / translation drills / listening exercises

### MVP success criteria

After 90 days from launch:
- **1,000+ free signups** (proves the funnel works)
- **30+ Pro subscribers** (3% conversion at this stage = validation)
- **£2,400+ MRR** by month 3 (covers infra cost and proves willingness-to-pay)

If those hit, build GCSE tier next. If they don't, the issue isn't paywall — it's product/market fit, and we need to fix that before adding more tiers.

## The deeper principle

There's a saying in subscription businesses: **"Free isn't your marketing — it's your product."** People who would pay convert in their own time when they're ready. The free experience's job is to keep them around long enough for that moment to arrive.

A hard paywall on day one says: "Decide right now whether I'm worth £8/mo, with almost no information." A generous free tier says: "Use this for a month, build a habit, then decide." Heritage learners need the second version.

## Cross-device free — yes, you're right

It's 2026 — multi-device sync is an expectation, not a feature. Heritage households are exactly the case: kid on iPhone, mum on iPad, dad on a laptop at work, all sharing one akhar account in spirit. Gating that creates friction with no upside (Supabase syncs automatically the moment they're signed in — costs us nothing to enable).

Withholding it would feel punitive in a way that "audio downloads" or "AI marking" don't. Make it free.

## Save-to-deck paid — I'd split the difference

You're directionally right that "save" is a strong engagement signal — but the actual learning value isn't in *saving* a word, it's in **reviewing** it with spaced repetition. The thing tutors and language schools charge for isn't the word list — it's the active recall loop.

Three reasons to make **saving free but reviewing paid**:

1. **Saving is a habit-formation hook.** A user who saves their first 10 words is dramatically more likely to keep using the app than one who doesn't. Free saves = more engaged users = better conversion later. Paywalling the save itself prevents the very behaviour that builds paying users.

2. **Heritage learners save sentimentally.** "I want to remember ਨਾਨੀ because grandma used to say it." Putting a paywall on that emotional moment is a really bad first impression. They'll bounce.

3. **The killer feature is the review loop, not the list.** Anki has unlimited free saving — it's a giant market leader despite that. What people actually pay for is the *structured review experience*: FSRS scheduling, daily review session, audio playback during review, performance analytics, custom decks grouped by theme. That's where real learning happens, and that's what justifies £8/mo.

**My counter-proposal:**

| Action | Tier |
|---|---|
| See a saved-words list (passive) | Free |
| Save words from any sakhi or lesson | Free |
| Hear audio for a saved word | Free |
| **Daily SRS review session with FSRS scheduling** | **Pro** |
| Custom decks (group by theme, sakhi, etc.) | Pro |
| Performance analytics (retention curve, weak words) | Pro |
| Audio-only review mode for commutes | Pro |
| Export deck to Anki | Pro |

So the free user gets a "vocabulary scrapbook." The paid user gets a "personal Punjabi memory system." Different products, both valuable, clear upgrade reason.

- 5 sakhis fully open (hover, audio, save-to-deck)
- **Cross-device sync** ✅
- **Save unlimited words to a personal list** ✅
- Streaming audio

### MVP Pro — £8/mo or £80/yr
- All ~50 processed sakhis
- **Daily SRS review session** (the active learning loop)
- Custom decks

- Deck analytics

### Out of MVP
- GCSE / A-Level tiers
- AI marking
- Beginner readers
- Native apps
- Family Plan

## Alternative if you genuinely want save = paid

If you feel strongly that the "moment of intent" is the right conversion point (Headspace/Calm-style), we could go more aggressive:

### Alternative MVP Free

- 5 sakhis with hover + audio (no save)

This is simpler to message ("Pro = remember what you learn") and might convert faster but loses the habit-formation hook. Worth A/B testing once we have volume, not at launch.

Go with the **split** (save free, review paid). It maps cleanly to how Anki vs Memrise vs LingQ differentiate. The save-to-deck button stays as a moment of delight on the free tier; the SRS review at `/deck` is gated with a clear "Start your daily review" upsell.

## You're right that 58 lessons is a lot

The whole alphabet curriculum took 5 days of work and is genuinely high quality. Giving it away entirely is the Duolingo move, which made sense when I was thinking purely about SEO. But you're correct that for a £8/mo product with a small market, we need *something* to gate even within the script section.

## The clean split: "recognise" free, "read" paid

The 58 lessons fall into two pedagogical halves:

**Half 1 — "I can identify Punjabi letters" (~39 lessons)**
- Pronunciation primer
- 35 paintee akhar (the letters themselves)
- 5 nukta letters
- Reference chart
- Recognition exercise

After this, a learner can *look at any Punjabi text and name each letter*. They can't read it yet — because they don't know vowel signs.

**Half 2 — "I can actually read Punjabi" (~19 lessons)**
- Mukta (inherent 'a')
- 9 matras (Kannā ā, Sihārī i, Bihārī ī, Aunkaṛ u, Dulæṅkaṛ ū, Lāvāṅ e, Dulāvāṅ æ, Hōṛā o, Kanɔṛā ɔ)
- 5 diacritic concepts (Adhikk, Tippī, Bindī, Pairī Rārā, Tone-H)
- 4 story lessons (Kulbir's day, Flying birds, Clever crow, Vaisakhi)
- Glossary

This is the half that makes you a reader. **Gate it behind Pro.**

## Why this split is honest, not arbitrary

1. **It maps to what people Google.** "Punjabi alphabet" → free (we own that SEO term). "Punjabi vowel signs" / "how to read Gurmukhi" → paid. Both terms exist, both have intent, but the second one has stronger conversion intent.

2. **It mirrors how the original book is sold.** JS Nagra's Panjabi Made Easy Book 1 is £8 at the SikhBookClub. We're giving away the equivalent of pages 5–24 (the letter pages) free and gating pages 25–48 (matras + diacritics + stories). Honest framing: "the first half of the book is free."

3. **Heritage learners who already read some Punjabi don't need the matra lessons** — they're reading by recognition already. They land on free, browse the alphabet refresher, then go straight to the 5 free sakhis. Their entry point is reading, not the curriculum.

4. **Beginners who are learning from scratch hit a clear wall**: "you've learned the letters; to actually read words, unlock vowel signs with Pro." This is the cleanest possible conversion moment — they're invested, they understand the gap, they see the path forward.

5. **One teaser matra free.** Unlock Kannā (the long ā) free so beginners *understand what a matra is and how it works* before they're asked to pay. Then the other 8 + diacritics are gated. Babbel and Memrise both do this — first lesson of each course free, rest paywalled.

## Updated MVP free tier

- Pronunciation primer
- 35 letters + nukta + chart + recognition exercise
- **1 matra lesson** (Kannā, the long ā) — the teaser
- 5 sakhis fully open (hover, audio, save-to-deck)
- **Cross-device sync** ✅ (from last round)
- **Save unlimited words to personal list** ✅ (from last round)
- Streaming audio
